newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-NORRIS, TRINIDAD KEEP TITLES, RANDALL UPSET IN NASHVILLE.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-NORRIS, TRINIDAD KEEP TITLES, RANDALL UPSET IN NASHVILLE.

text.p: Terry Norris held onto his junior middleweight titles on Saturday by pummeling Canadian challenger Nick Rupa, who stood up to more punishment than seemed humanly possible before the fight was stopped in the 10th round.
The card featured four title fights but only one major surprise, when American Frankie Randall was stunned by Khalid Rahilou of France to lose his World Boxing Association junior welterweight crown.
Undefeated International Boxing Federation welterweight champion Felix Trinidad came off the canvas in the second round and put away Briton Kevin Lueshing in the third.
And Henry Akinwande retained the lightly-regarded World Boxing Organisation heavyweight crown with a lopsided, but lackluster decision over fellow Briton Scott Welch.
Norris threw everything he had at Rupa to keep his World Boxing Council and IBF titles.
Rupa was staggered in the fourth round and Norris landed thundering punches to the Canadian's head throughout before finally knocking him down twice in the 10th round.
The referee stopped the fight at 2:34 of the 10th, but the courageous Rupa seemed ready to get back up and take more punishment from the champion.
"I hit him with a lot of shots that would have knocked down anybody, but he stayed in there. I take my hat off to him," Norris said.
"I was trying to hit him with everything," added Norris, who raised his record to 45-6.
"It was a great fight by Terry. I just walked into a few," said Rupa. "When my eye started closing up it was hard to see that right coming."
Trinidad improved to 31-0 despite a slow start.
Trinidad got his wakeup call in the second round when Lueshing put the champion on the seat of his pants with a left hook in the second round.
But Trinidad came roaring back in the third, sending Lueshing (19-2) crashing to the canvas three times.
The third knockdown came when Trinidad landed a devastating left hook to the jaw just before the bell and the referee halted the battering with Lueshing on his back and one second left in the third.
"I felt the punch that knocked me down, but I got up and took care of business," Trinidad said. "I was confident I was going to win when I got up.
"Conditioning got me through it," added Trinidad, who has made 11 successful title defences.
Said Lueshing: "I let him off the hook. That was a good learning experience for me."
Randall, who has a reputation for less than Spartan training habits, paid the price Saturday, appearing lethargic and slow on his feet.
Rahilou allowed Randall to expend a lot of energy early and went to work after the defending champion began to appear arm weary midway through the bout.
In the 11th round Rahilou landed more than 20 unanswered punches to Randall's head, moving the champion into a corner, where the punishment continued.
The referee stopped the bout at 58 seconds of the round, giving the Frenchman the crown in his first world title fight.
"I was too strong for him," said Rahilou, who improved to 29-2.
Randall (53-5-1) was clearly surprised by the Frenchman's ability and fitness.
"He was in top condition," Randall said. "I wasn't on, it wasn't my night.
"I'm not over the hill, I'm not finished. I'm still good," insisted Randall, whose defeat likely cost him a shot at lucrative unification bouts.
Akinwande (31-0-1) won every round but was frustrated by Welch's constant holding and refusal to trade punches, which kept Akinwande from scoring the knockout he badly wanted.
"As you can see he doesn't want to fight," complained Akinwande, who now lives and trains in Florida.
"He kept holding on when the referee said break."
